title: Breaking News Homepage
prompt: A news site's homepage is read far more often than its database can serve. Editors want breaking news to appear on the homepage quickly. Design the read path for the homepage.
facts: Peak: about 20,000 homepage reads per second
The database serves about 2,000 reads per second and should run at no more than two thirds of that at peak
A new story must appear on the homepage within 30 seconds of publishing
Building the homepage from the database takes at most 2 seconds, including storing it in the cache
The homepage is the same for every reader
scope: Article pages and personalization are out of scope

requirements: States the 30-second freshness requirement and the database limit
Notes that every reader sees the same page, so one cache key serves everyone
estimation: Allowed misses: 1,333 ÷ 20,000 ≈ 6.7%, so a hit rate of at least about 93%
Freshness: a cached copy can be up to 2 s old when stored, so the TTL is at most 30 − 2 = 28 s
design: Servers read the homepage from a cache (cache-aside or a refresh job) before the database
data: One cache key for the homepage with a TTL of at most 28 seconds, or a job that rebuilds it every few seconds
Explains why the hit rate stays high: one key read 20,000 times per second misses only when it expires
tradeoffs: Names the thundering-herd risk at expiry with its condition: when the key expires, many servers miss at once and hit the database; one rebuild at a time, or a background refresh, prevents it
Or: a shorter TTL gives fresher news but more rebuilds

fullMarkDesigns: Cache-aside: servers read the homepage key from the cache; on a miss one server rebuilds it (others serve the old copy) and stores it with a TTL of 25 s. Hit rate is close to 100% because one key serves every reader. Risk: thundering herd at expiry, handled by letting only one server rebuild.

A background job rebuilds the homepage every 10 s and writes it to the cache; servers only read the cache and never call the database for the homepage. Database load is one build every 10 s. Freshness: at most 10 s between rebuilds + 2 s to build = 12 s, within 30 s. Trade-off: the job is a new part that must be watched; if it stops, the page goes stale.

assumptions: Every reader gets the same homepage
The cache is in the same data center as the servers
reference.design:
Servers read the homepage from the cache. On a miss, a single server rebuilds it from the database (at most 2 s) and stores it with a TTL of 25 s; other servers keep serving the previous copy until the new one is ready.
Database budget: 2,000 × 2 ÷ 3 ≈ 1,333 reads per second, so at most about 6.7% of 20,000 reads may miss. With one key, misses happen only at expiry, so the hit rate is close to 100%.
Freshness: a copy can be 2 s old when stored and lives 25 s, so news appears within about 27 s, inside 30 s.
alternatives: A CDN for the homepage HTML with a short TTL: removes even more load, with the same freshness limit
Invalidating the key when an editor publishes: fresher, but every publish must reach the cache reliably

title: Travel Blog Photos Worldwide
prompt: A travel blog stores its photos on one origin server in Singapore. Readers in Europe and the United States complain that photos load slowly. Design how photos are delivered.
facts: About 2 million photo requests per day, from Asia, Europe and the United States
A round trip from Europe or the United States to Singapore takes about 160–220 ms
Photos never change after upload; an edited photo is uploaded under a new file name
Requirement: a photo that was already requested in a reader's region recently loads within 300 ms
The origin server can send about 300 photos per second
scope: The blog's text pages are out of scope

requirements: States the 300 ms requirement and that it applies to photos already requested in the region, not the very first request
estimation: Average load: 2 × 10⁶ ÷ 10⁵ = 20 photos per second, within the origin's 300 even without a CDN, so the problem is distance, not load
Or: a request that must cross to Singapore needs at least one 160–220 ms round trip, often two with a new connection, so meeting 300 ms needs a nearby copy
design: Readers → CDN edge server in their region → origin in Singapore on a miss
data: Long TTL (days or longer) because photos never change, and new versions get new names (versioned file names)
Explains the first request in a region is a miss and goes to the origin
tradeoffs: Names a trade-off with its condition, such as: the first request for a photo in each region is slow, which the requirement allows
Or: a deleted or wrong photo stays on edges until it expires, so the team needs a purge or short TTL for removals

fullMarkDesigns: Put a CDN in front of the origin. Photos are cached at edges near readers with a long TTL; edited photos get new file names, so no invalidation is needed. Load is only about 20 photos per second, so the origin is fine; the CDN fixes distance. First request per region goes to Singapore and may be slow.

Store photos in object storage behind a CDN, with versioned names and a one-year TTL. Edges in Europe and the US serve repeat requests in tens of milliseconds. Trade-off: removing a photo needs a CDN purge, because edges keep it until the TTL ends.

assumptions: Most photos are read many times in each region
The CDN has edge servers in Europe and the United States
reference.design:
Readers fetch photos from a CDN. The nearest edge server returns a cached copy; on a miss it fetches the photo from the origin in Singapore and keeps it.
Because photos never change and an edit gets a new file name, the TTL can be very long, so edges almost never go back to the origin.
Load is about 2 × 10⁶ ÷ 10⁵ = 20 photos per second, far below the origin's 300; the slowness comes from 160–220 ms round trips, which the edge removes for repeat requests.
The first request for a photo in a region still crosses to Singapore, which the requirement allows.
alternatives: A second origin server in Europe: fixes Europe only and must be kept in sync
Short TTLs: allow quick removal, but more requests go back to Singapore
